extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate CS students (CS103) learning to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: A beginner-friendly guide to writing standard mathematical proofs used in CS103: templates and conventions for direct proofs, proofs involving quantifiers, biconditionals, and indirect proofs (contrapositive, contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof of an implication (assume antecedent, prove consequent)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement of the form 'If P then Q' by direct proof: assume the antecedent P is true and prove the consequent Q is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure your proof with an explicit assume step and a want-to-show step (e.g., 'Assume x is a pizkwat. We need to show x is a squigglebah'). Provide the actual line of reasoning manipulating what you have from the assume step until you arrive at the want-to-show, then explicitly indicate you have reached the goal and close the proof (e.g., 'Thus x is a squigglebah, which is what we needed to show. ■'). Alternate phrasings that are acceptable: 'Suppose', 'Let x be', 'We will show that...'. The important thing is to clearly state you are assuming the antecedent and that you will prove the consequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof structure: explicit steps (assume, want-to-show, reasoning, close)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a four-part narrative arc in direct proofs: (1) write your assume step, (2) write your want-to-show step, (3) write the actual reasoning, (4) return to your want-to-show and end the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make each part explicit so the reader can follow the intended flow. The guide emphasizes not skipping the announcement of assumptions or the concluding statement that you have reached the want-to-show. Ending with a clear closing sentence and a box/■ is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of a universally-quantified statement (pick arbitrary object)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements of the form 'For all objects of type T, property R holds', instruct the reader to pick an arbitrary object of that type and show it has the required property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a sentence like 'Pick a natural number n' or 'Let n ∈ ℕ be an arbitrary natural number.' This indicates you are not choosing a specific element. Then state the want-to-show for that arbitrary object, do the reasoning using properties common to that type of object, and finally call back to the want-to-show and close (e.g., 'Thus n is the sum of four perfect squares, as required. ■'). Equivalent phrasings include 'Consider', 'Let', 'Fix', or 'Choose'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of an existential statement (give a witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement of the form 'There exists an object with property R', explicitly construct or specify a witness and prove it satisfies the required properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ask the reader to pick an arbitrary object. Instead write something like 'Pick x = ... . We need to show x is a swipestone and x is edurable.' Then prove those properties and conclude. The key difference from universal proofs is that you must provide a concrete example (the witness) rather than an arbitrary element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling nested quantifiers (unpacking universal + existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a universally-quantified statement contains an existential claim (e.g., 'For any n there exist r and s such that ...'), first pick an arbitrary outer object, then show existence by constructing appropriate inner witnesses depending on that outer object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template: 'Pick some integer n. We want to show there are integers r and s where r^2 - s^2 = 4n. Pick r = ... and s = ... . Then prove the required equality. Thus ... as required. ■' The guide recommends sketching the structure even if you don't yet know the specific witness choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpacking compound statements (combine quantifier-introduction and antecedent-assumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements that mix quantifiers and implications (e.g., 'For any n, if P(n) then Q(n)'), you should unpack the outer quantifier then the inner implication, possibly combining steps for concision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard approach: pick an arbitrary object (e.g., 'Pick an integer n. We will show that if n is even then n^2 is even.'), then assume the antecedent ('Assume n is even') and proceed to prove the consequent. You may also combine the introduction and assumption (e.g., 'Pick an even integer n. We will show n^2 is even'), which is logically equivalent and often cleaner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of a biconditional (prove both directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'P if and only if Q', treat it as two implications and prove each direction separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by picking an arbitrary object (if needed) and state you'll prove both directions. Then provide a proof that P ⇒ Q (using any suitable technique) and a separate proof that Q ⇒ P. Conclude with a single end-of-proof marker (■). The guide explicitly suggests you can use any technique (direct, contrapositive, contradiction) within each direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive (announce and prove the contrapositive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of proving 'If P then Q' directly, prove its contrapositive 'If not Q then not P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always start by announcing you're proving the contrapositive (e.g., 'We will prove the contrapositive of this statement, namely, that ...') and explicitly write out the contrapositive. Do not skip this step. Then use any proof technique (often a direct proof) to prove the contrapositive—start by assuming ¬Q and show ¬P. This reduces the chance of taking the contrapositive incorrectly and communicates intent to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (explicit negation and derive an impossibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove X, assume ¬X and deduce a logical contradiction; conclude that X must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by announcing it's a proof by contradiction and explicitly write the negation of the statement you're proving (e.g., 'Assume for the sake of contradiction that ...'). From that assumption, derive an impossible statement (e.g., 1=0, an element of the empty set, or a logical contradiction). State that you've reached a contradiction and, if not obvious, explain why it is impossible. Then conclude (e.g., 'We have reached a contradiction, so our assumption must have been wrong, so ...'). The guide emphasizes carefully forming negations and provides a helpful table of common statement types with their negations to avoid mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation rules for common statement types (aid for contradiction proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for forming negations of common logical statements, to be used when setting up proofs by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists a table mapping patterns to their negations, e.g.: 'All P's are Q's' ⇄ assume 'Some P is not a Q'; 'No P's are Q's' ⇄ 'Some P is a Q'; 'If P then Q' ⇄ assume 'P is true and Q is false', etc. Use these rules to write the correct negation before attempting a contradiction proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of language and announcing proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Always communicate to the reader what proof technique you are using and the steps you will take (e.g., state 'We will prove the contrapositive' or 'Assume for the sake of contradiction that ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly announcing plan helps the reader follow your argument and prevents mistakes (e.g., incorrect contrapositives or negations). The guide recommends not skipping these announcements, and gives several acceptable phrasings for variable introduction and assumptions (e.g., 'Pick', 'Consider', 'Let', 'Fix').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude by returning to the want-to-show and close explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing the core reasoning, explicitly indicate you have achieved the want-to-show and end the proof clearly (often with 'Thus ... as required.' and a box/■).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This closing sentence closes the narrative arc of the proof and signals completion to the reader. It is part of good proof-writing etiquette and should not be omitted.
